query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially replacing Mo with additional Nb in equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo will reduce the excessive electronegativity difference that currently hinders dislocation motion, thereby enhancing room‐temperature ductility while largely retaining the high strength provided by solid‐solution strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo high-entropy alloy that forms a disordered BCC solid solution, exhibiting a high compressive yield strength (~1719 MPa) but limited room-temperature plasticity, where the high Mo content contributes to a larger electronegativity difference.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by partially substituting Mo with Nb (e.g. synthesizing an alloy of composition NbZrTiHfMo_(1-x)Nb_(x) with a moderate substitution level such as x ≈ 0.1–0.2) so that the overall Mo content is reduced while extra Nb is provided.
generation.conditions: The alloy would be fabricated via arc melting followed by homogenization treatment. Room-temperature compressive tests would be performed at a quasi-static strain rate (∼10^–3 s^–1) under ambient atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: A disordered BCC solid-solution lattice with reduced lattice distortions caused by a smaller electronegativity mismatch, which facilitates dislocation motion and promotes plasticity.
generation.mechanism: By reducing the Mo content, the alloy experiences a lower electronegativity mismatch and decreased local bonding heterogeneity. This adjustment lessens the lattice barriers for dislocation movement, thereby enhancing ductility. The additional Nb, known to be beneficial for ductility in similar refractory systems, helps maintain sufficient solid-solution strengthening to retain high yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in the ductility (plastic strain increase by approximately 20% or more) at room temperature, with a minimal decrease (less than about 10%) in compressive yield strength compared to the baseline equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy with a reported compressive yield strength of about 1719 MPa and limited room-temperature plasticity.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only over a composition range where Mo reduction does not exceed a critical level that would otherwise compromise solid-solution strengthening. The intervention is tuned for room-temperature compression behavior; its effects at high temperatures or under other loading conditions remain to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies suggest that increasing Nb can improve ductility in refractory HEAs, the precise substitution level that optimally balances strength and plasticity is uncertain and may require fine-tuning. Quantitative improvements are approximate given the complex interplay among elemental effects in high-entropy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys with varying degrees of Mo substitution by Nb (e.g. x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 in NbZrTiHfMo_(1-x)Nb_(x)). Process the alloys by arc melting and homogenization. Conduct room-temperature uniaxial compression tests at a quasi-static strain rate (∼10^–3 s^–1) and perform microstructural characterization (using SEM, TEM, and XRD) to confirm phase stability and lattice parameters.
measurements: Microstructural features (grain size, homogeneity, phase analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloys do not show a substantial improvement in plasticity (an increase of less than 5% in plastic strain) or if the yield strength decreases by more than 10% relative to the baseline equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
